inline_comments.comment: `getGitDir` unconditionally appends `.git` to the repo root, but in a git worktree `.git` is a regular file, not a directory. Calling `watch('/repo/.git/HEAD', ...)` when `.git` is a file will throw `ENOTDIR` (not `ENOENT`), which bubbles out of `watchFile` and is then silently swallowed by `setupWatchers`'s broad catch. The result is that all three watchers are silently never started for any user of git worktrees — the feature degrades to no-op with no feedback. Using `git rev-parse --git-dir` (already available via `execa`) instead of `join(repoRoot, '.git')` would return the real git directory path in all layouts, including worktrees.

The `Object.keys(this.watchers).length > 0` guard prevents re-running setup when watchers already exist. However, if `setupWatchers` runs `watchFile('head', ...)` and `watchFile('packedRefs', ...)` successfully but then errors partway through `configureBranchWatcher` (e.g., a non-ENOENT readFile failure), the outer `catch` in `setupWatchers` silences the error and sets `watcherSetupInFlight = undefined`. On the next call to `ensureWatchers`, this guard finds two watchers in `this.watchers` and returns early — so the branch watcher is permanently missing and can never be re-attempted. Consider clearing all watchers in the `catch` branch (or not early-returning when partially set up) so a subsequent call can retry from a clean state.

The broad `catch` block silences all errors from watcher setup with only a terse comment. If watching silently fails (e.g., because of the worktree ENOTDIR issue, a permission problem, or git not being accessible), users have no indication that the git-state-change trigger is inactive and will wonder why committed changes still show as modified. A `logger.debug(...)` call here (similar to how other unavailability conditions are logged elsewhere in the service) would make diagnosing failures much easier.

`isEnoentError` only matches `ENOENT`. When the `.git` path component is a file rather than a directory (git worktrees), `node:fs`'s `watch` throws with code `ENOTDIR`. This error is not caught here, re-throws from `watchFile`, and is then silently swallowed by `setupWatchers`'s outer catch. It would be clearer to also handle `ENOTDIR` explicitly here (or in `isEnoentError`) rather than relying on the distant outer catch for this expected case.

The regex capture group `(.+)` can include a trailing `\r` on Windows when git writes CRLF line endings. For example, `.git/HEAD` might contain `ref: refs/heads/main\r\n`; after `.trim()` on the full string it becomes `ref: refs/heads/main\r`, and the capture group yields `refs/heads/main\r`. `join(gitDir, 'refs/heads/main\r')` then produces a path that does not exist, so the branch watcher is silently never registered. Trimming `match[1]` (e.g., `match[1].trim()`) before returning it would close this gap.

The option type was changed from `Pick<GitDiffProvider, 'getChangedFiles' | 'getRepoRoot'>` to the concrete `GitDiffProvider` class. The previous `Pick` type served as an implicit interface, making it easy to pass any object with the right shape. Now callers must provide an actual `GitDiffProvider` instance (or a subclass), which is why the test had to introduce `MockGitDiffProvider extends GitDiffProvider`. Extracting a `GitDiffProviderLike` interface (or keeping a structural `Pick` type that includes `onGitStateChange`) would keep the boundary structural and make the contract more explicit without requiring subclassing in tests or alternative consumers.

`void callback` is a no-op expression statement — it evaluates `callback` (a function parameter) and discards the result, having no observable effect. The intent appears to be suppressing an unused-variable warning, but the idiomatic TypeScript/ESLint way to signal an intentionally unused parameter is to prefix it with an underscore: `_callback`. Consider renaming the parameter in the `vi.fn(...)` initializer to `(_callback) => { ... }` (or just dropping the parameter entirely) to make the intent clear.

general_comments.comment: There is no test covering the scenario where a git state change fires before the first module graph has been received. In that case, `onGitStateChange`'s callback in `ChangeDetectionService` calls `scheduleScan(debounceMs)`, a timer fires, and `scan()` returns immediately because `!this.latestModuleGraph`. The behavior is safe, but it is an untested code path. Adding a test that fires an `onGitStateChange` event before the first `emit(moduleGraph)` and asserts that `getChangedFilesMock` is NOT called would document and protect this invariant.

Replacing the ad-hoc inline mock objects (`{ getChangedFiles: vi.fn(), getRepoRoot: vi.fn() }`) with the typed `MockGitDiffProvider` class is a clear improvement — mock setup is now centralized, discoverable through named mock properties, and type-checked. One caveat: because `MockGitDiffProvider` extends the production class, any future constructor change to `GitDiffProvider` (e.g., making `cwd` required) silently affects tests via the hardcoded `super('/repo')`. If the service option is later refactored to accept an interface, the mock could implement that interface directly instead of subclassing, which would be more resilient to production class changes.
